title: Solaris
full_review:
A cry for help from a space station under siege brings a widowed psychologist on board in the melancholy tale "Solaris" (20th Century Fox).

Something is very amiss at the space station monitoring the planet Solaris. Back on Earth, grieving widower Dr. Chris Kelvin (George Clooney) receives an urgent video plea from his friend, the ship's commander (Ulrich Tukur), that something unspecified has imperiled all on board and for him to please come at once.

Upon his arrival, Kelvin finds that, of the four crew, one is missing, another has committed suicide, while jittery Snow (Jeremy Davies) talks in circles and paranoid Gordon (Viola Davis) is hostile to Kelvin's questions. She warns him not to trust the experiences he is about to have.

When Kelvin sleeps he dreams of his wife, Rheya (Natascha McElhone), who had killed herself, leaving Kelvin devastated and filled with guilt. To his shock, when he awakes Rheya is beside him. Mistrusting his senses he tries to eject her into space but she soon reappears and Kelvin starts warming to the idea that, hallucination or not, this is his second chance. Gordon warns him otherwise -- and Rheya does not seem happy, either. The discovery of a body and a stolen identity pushes Gordon to make a fateful decision.

Using Stanislaw Lem's science-fiction novel and Andrei Tarkovsky's 1972 same-titled film as a starting point, Steven Soderbergh wrote the screenplay and directed the film in strikingly minimalist fashion. The claustrophobic quality of the cinematography mirrors the confined fears in the protagonists' minds as they try to distinguish fantasy from reality and ponder thorny metaphysical questions.

But that doesn't mean "Solaris" will prove an interesting movie for many in the audience. Initially intriguing, the mysterious premise gradually gives way to a sluggish pace and dreary tone that become oppressive.

Using continuous flashbacks, the filmmaker fills us in on how Kelvin and Rheya met and married, but is less clear about why she overdosed after possibly having an abortion and deciding he no longer loved her.

Saddled with difficult roles, Clooney and McElhone do their best to convey emotional turmoil, but the vagueness of the dialogue and the chilly visuals eventually distance the viewer. The cerebral script muses about the connection between love and death and mystical suggestions about the afterlife, but the movie fails to remain emotionally involving. Nor should Catholics expect a conventional spiritual interpretation of life after death.

It's a rare sci-fi movie that has no real action scenes or flurry of special effects, but in this case they might have added some needed energy to the increasingly gloomy proceedings.

However, some may find this somber meditation on grief, regrets and mind games to be a bracingly different addition to the sci-fi genre.

Due to a shadowy sexual encounter, brief rear nudity and off-screen violence, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
